newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian opposition leads presidential poll.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian opposition leads presidential poll.

text.p: Opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov has taken a decisive first round lead over his Socialist rival in Bulgaria's weekend presidential election, preliminary results on Monday showed.
An electoral commission official told Reuters Stoyanov was leading with 43.65 percent of the vote, while Culture Minister Ivan Marazov had 27.07 percent.
Colourful former emigre George Ganchev, leader of the Bulgarian Business Bloc, was third with 22.18 percent.
The official declined to specify what percentage of votes had been counted so far but the results conformed closely to projections from private polling agencies.
If full results show no candidate has an absolute majority, a second round will be held on Sunday. The commission has said it will announce more figures later in the day.
Monday's newspapers described Stoyanov's lead as a stinging blow to the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) government, which many voters blame for the unprecedented economic crisis.
"There is no winner but we know who the loser is," said Troud daily.

Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov has a secure majority in parliament -- where real power in Bulgaria lies -- but the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces currently holds the more ceremonial post of president.

Rifts within Socialist ranks have become more public since the still unsolved October 2 killing of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov, and whilst parliament is only half way through its four-year term, the election debacle is expected to prompt changes within the party.
Party officials said the Socialists were meeting on Monday morning to discuss their next move.
"The BSP has lost elections before but never by such a wide margin," said Kontinent daily.

Standart daily commented that the opposition had scored about the same vote as in the December 1994 parliamentary elections, while the Socialists, who won the parliamentary poll, had lost votes this time to the populist Ganchev, who styles himself as the alternative to the two main parties.
"The overwhelming victory of Petar Stoyanov in the first round showed that voters rejected this cabinet's policy and its inability to rule," said an editorial.
"In the last parliamentary elections, around 2.3 million Bulgarians voted for the BSP, now they are half as many."
The reform laggard of the ex-Warsaw Pact east European countries, this largely agricultural nation of just 8.4 million people has been slow to shake off its communist legacy.
It has the lowest level of foreign investment of any country in the region and a quarter of its numerous and insolvent banks are in receivership.
The central bank is rapidly running out of money to prop up the lev and buy fuel and wheat to prevent shortages during the coming winter.
Prices are rising, the lev is falling, interest rates are around 240 percent and foreign exchange reserves have plunged to about $505 million from $1.5 billion a year ago.
The lev firmed slightly to 240 per dollar on Monday morning from 240-243 at Friday's close but dealers said the election results were having no immediate impact.
